units.title: Hand Rankings
units.tip: Poker hands are ranked by rarity and strength. A royal flush beats everything. You need to instantly recognize which hand wins any showdown. Memorizing the rankings from highest to lowest is the first skill.

exercises.question: What is a royal flush?
exercises.answer: Ace, King, Queen, Jack, 10 all the same suit
exercises.explain: A royal flush is the rarest and strongest hand. It is the top of a straight flush sequence.
choices: Ace, King, Queen, Jack, 10 all the same suit
Any five cards of the same suit
Five cards in order, same suit

exercises.question: What is a straight flush?
exercises.answer: Five cards in order, all the same suit
exercises.explain: A straight flush is five consecutive cards of the same suit. A 9-8-7-6-5 of hearts is a straight flush. A royal flush is the best straight flush.
choices: Any flush that beats a straight
Three of a kind in one suit
Two pairs of the same suit
Five cards in order, all the same suit

exercises.question: What is four of a kind?
exercises.answer: All four cards of one rank, plus one other card
exercises.explain: Four of a kind is four cards of the same rank: four Kings, four 7s, etc. The fifth card is only used as a tiebreaker when two hands have the same four of a kind.
choices: Four cards with two matching suits
All four cards of one rank, plus one other card

exercises.question: What is a full house?
exercises.answer: Three of a kind plus a pair
exercises.explain: A full house is three cards of one rank and two cards of another rank. Kings and 7s (K-K-K-7-7) is a full house.
choices: Two pairs plus a single card
Three of a kind plus a pair
Any three cards of the same suit

exercises.question: What is a flush?
exercises.answer: Five cards all of the same suit, in any order
exercises.explain: A flush is any five cards of the same suit. They do not need to be in order. An Ace-high flush beats a King-high flush.
choices: Five cards all of the same suit, in any order
Any three cards of the same suit
Two pairs of the same suit

exercises.question: What is a straight?
exercises.answer: Five cards in order, any suits
exercises.explain: A straight is five consecutive cards. 9-8-7-6-5 is a straight. The suits do not matter. An Ace can be high (in 10-J-Q-K-A) or low (in A-2-3-4-5).
choices: Five cards in order, any suits
Five cards of the same suit

exercises.question: What beats a three of a kind in a showdown?
exercises.answer: A straight, flush, full house, four of a kind, or straight flush
exercises.explain: Three of a kind is fourth from the bottom of the ladder (high card, pair, two pair, three of a kind). The five hand types above it beat it: straight, flush, full house, four of a kind, and straight flush. Two pair, one pair, and high card lose to three of a kind.
choices: A straight, flush, full house, four of a kind, or straight flush
A pair with a high kicker
Two pair, or a pair of Aces

exercises.question: In a showdown with two pairs, which pair ranks higher?
exercises.answer: The higher-ranked pair determines the winner
exercises.explain: Kings and 5s beats Queens and 10s because Kings are ranked higher than Queens. If both players have the same two pairs, the highest fifth card (kicker) wins.
choices: The higher-ranked pair determines the winner
The pair that appears first on the board
The pair with the highest suit

exercises.question: What is a kicker?
exercises.answer: The highest unpaired card that breaks a tie
exercises.explain: When two players have the same hand (like a pair of 7s), the kicker is the highest other card. An Ace-kicker beats a King-kicker.
choices: The highest unpaired card that breaks a tie

exercises.question: Which hand is stronger: a pair of Aces or a pair of Kings?
exercises.answer: A pair of Aces
exercises.explain: Aces are the highest rank, so a pair of Aces beats every other pair. Suits never break ties in poker.

units.title: Game Structure
units.tip: Texas Hold'em has a fixed betting sequence. Small blind and big blind post first. The community cards come in stages: the flop (3 cards), the turn (1 card), the river (1 card). Each stage has betting, and players can fold, call, or raise.

exercises.question: What are the blinds in Texas Hold'em?
exercises.answer: Forced bets posted before cards are dealt
exercises.explain: The small blind (SB) and big blind (BB) are mandatory bets. The player to the left of the dealer posts the small blind, and the next player posts the big blind. They ensure there is a pot to play for.
choices: Forced bets posted before cards are dealt

exercises.question: Which statement about the two blinds is correct?
exercises.answer: The big blind is the larger of the two forced bets
exercises.explain: The big blind is the larger forced bet and the small blind is typically about half of it. A 1-2 game has blinds of 1 and 2, but some games use other ratios, such as 1-3.
choices: Both blinds are posted after the flop
The big blind is the larger of the two forced bets
The small blind is the larger bet
The two blinds are always equal

exercises.question: What is pre-flop betting?
exercises.answer: Betting before any community cards are shown
exercises.explain: Pre-flop happens after the blinds are posted and each player has two hole cards. Everyone acts in order, starting with the player after the big blind, and can fold, call, or raise.
choices: Betting before any community cards are shown

exercises.question: What is the flop?
exercises.answer: The first three community cards dealt together
exercises.explain: After pre-flop betting ends, the dealer burns a card and flops three cards face-up. These cards are shared by all remaining players.
choices: The first three community cards dealt together

exercises.question: After the flop is revealed, what happens next?
exercises.answer: Betting occurs, then the turn card is revealed
exercises.explain: Players bet on the flop. After all betting is done, the dealer burns a card and reveals the fourth community card, the turn.
choices: The hand ends in a showdown
All cards are revealed at once
Betting occurs, then the turn card is revealed

exercises.question: What is the turn?
exercises.answer: The fourth community card, revealed after flop betting
exercises.explain: After the flop betting round ends, the turn (also called fourth street) is dealt. It is a single card added to the board.
choices: The first card of the flop
The fourth community card, revealed after flop betting

exercises.question: What is the river?
exercises.answer: The fifth and final community card
exercises.explain: After turn betting, the river (also called fifth street) is dealt. It is the last card to come. After the river, there is one more betting round, then the showdown.
choices: The fifth and final community card

exercises.question: How many community cards are there in Texas Hold'em?
exercises.answer: Five
exercises.explain: Three on the flop, one on the turn, and one on the river. Combined with your two hole cards, you have seven cards total to make your best five-card hand.

exercises.question: What happens in a showdown?
exercises.answer: Players reveal their hole cards and the best hand wins the pot
exercises.explain: After the river betting round, if more than one player remains, they reveal their hole cards. The player with the best five-card hand wins the pot.
choices: Players reveal their hole cards and the best hand wins the pot

exercises.question: If one player bets on the river and everyone else folds, what happens?
exercises.answer: The remaining player wins the pot without showing cards
exercises.explain: You never have to show your cards if everyone folds. This is the key to bluffing: no one knows if you had the best hand.
choices: The player must show their cards
The remaining player wins the pot without showing cards
Everyone wins a portion of the pot

units.title: Position and Starting Hands
units.tip: Your position (where you sit relative to the dealer button) determines when you act. Earlier position means you act first, which is a disadvantage. Later position means you act last, which is an advantage. You can play more hands in late position than early position.

exercises.question: What is the dealer button?
exercises.answer: The marker that shows the dealer position, which acts last after the flop
exercises.explain: The button rotates clockwise after each hand. The player on the button acts last on the flop, turn, and river, which is the strongest position. Before the flop, the big blind acts last.
choices: The marker that shows the dealer position, which acts last after the flop

exercises.question: What is early position?
exercises.answer: Acting before most other players, which is a disadvantage
exercises.explain: Early position includes the player first to act before the flop (just after the big blind). You act with little information about other players' hands, so most players choose fewer hands from there.
choices: Acting before most other players, which is a disadvantage

exercises.question: What is late position?
exercises.answer: Acting after most other players, which is an advantage
exercises.explain: Late position includes the button and the cutoff (one seat before the button). You act with the most information. You can play more hands from late position.
choices: Acting after most other players, which is an advantage

exercises.question: Why is late position an advantage?
exercises.answer: You see other players act first, giving you information to decide
exercises.explain: Late position lets you react to what others do. You can fold weak hands, call strong hands, or raise to win the pot uncontested.
choices: You see other players act first, giving you information to decide

exercises.question: From which position can a player profitably play more hands?
exercises.answer: Late position, because you act with more information
exercises.explain: In early position, fewer hands are worth playing. In late position, more hands become profitable because you see what others do before you decide.
choices: Late position, because you act with more information
Early position, because there are fewer players left

exercises.question: What is a premium hand in early position?
exercises.answer: Pairs of Aces, Kings, Queens, or Ace-King
exercises.explain: Premium hands are strong before the flop and hold up well against multiple opponents. Most players are happy to play these hands from any position.
choices: Any two cards ten or higher
Pairs of Aces, Kings, Queens, or Ace-King

exercises.question: What does it mean to have a weak hand pre-flop?
exercises.answer: A hand unlikely to win without improvement
exercises.explain: Weak hands need help from the flop. A 7-4 offsuit is weak because it has low ranks, no pair, and no flush potential.
choices: A hand with only one high card
A hand with a low kicker
A hand unlikely to win without improvement

exercises.question: What is a connector?
exercises.answer: Two cards of consecutive rank, like 9-8 or J-10
exercises.explain: Connectors have draw potential because they can make straights. A 9-8 can make a straight with 7-6-5, 10-7-6, J-10-7, or Q-J-10, four different combinations.
choices: Two cards of consecutive rank, like 9-8 or J-10
Two cards of the same suit

exercises.question: What is a gapped hand?
exercises.answer: Two cards with a rank gap between them, like 9-7
exercises.explain: A gapped hand like 9-7 has one rank missing (the 8). It is weaker than a connector because it makes fewer straights: 9-7 can make three (with the 8 plus 5-6, 6-10, or 10-J), while 9-8 can make four.
choices: Two cards with a rank gap between them, like 9-7

exercises.question: What does suited mean for a starting hand?
exercises.answer: Both cards are the same suit, giving flush potential
exercises.explain: A suited hand like K-Q of hearts has flush potential. An unsuited K-Q can only make a flush if four board cards share a suit with one of your cards, which is rare. Suited hands are somewhat stronger than unsuited hands of the same ranks.
choices: Both cards are the same suit, giving flush potential
Both cards are the same rank

units.title: Pot Odds and Outs
units.tip: Pot odds compare the price of a call with the size of the pot. Count your outs (cards that improve your hand), estimate the chance of hitting one, and compare that chance with the share of the final pot you must put in. If your chance to win is higher than the share you must put in, the call has positive expectation.

exercises.question: If you have 9-8 and the flop is 7-5-2, how many cards make you a straight?
exercises.answer: Four cards: the four 6s
exercises.explain: A 6 completes 5-6-7-8-9, a straight. A Jack or a 10 does not complete a straight by itself, because you would still be missing another card. That leaves 4 outs, a gutshot draw.
choices: Five cards: 6, J, and one other
Eight cards: four 6s and four Jacks

exercises.question: What is an out?
exercises.answer: A card that improves your hand and helps you win
exercises.explain: Outs are the cards left in the deck that would improve your hand to a likely winner. For example, with four cards to a flush, the remaining cards of that suit are outs.
choices: A card that makes you fold
Any card you do not want
A card that improves your hand and helps you win

exercises.question: If you have 9-9 and the flop is K-Q-2, how many outs give you a set?
exercises.answer: Two cards: the remaining 9s
exercises.explain: You have a pair of 9s. The two other 9s in the deck will give you three of a kind (a set). You exclude the 9 in your hand.

exercises.question: What is a flush draw?
exercises.answer: Four cards of the same suit, needing one more for a flush
exercises.explain: A flush draw has four suited cards. There are 13 cards of each suit, so 9 cards remain to complete the flush (13 - 4 = 9).
choices: Four cards of the same suit, needing one more for a flush
Three cards of the same suit

exercises.question: If you have a flush draw on the turn, how many cards complete your flush on the river?
exercises.answer: Nine cards
exercises.explain: There are 13 cards in each suit. Four of that suit are visible (in your hand and on the board), which leaves 9 cards in the deck to complete the flush.

exercises.question: What are pot odds?
exercises.answer: The ratio of the pot size to the cost of your call
exercises.explain: If the pot is 100 and you need to call 20, your pot odds are 100 to 20, or 5 to 1. You win 100 if you win, risk 20 if you lose.
choices: The ratio of the pot size to the cost of your call

exercises.question: If the pot is 100 and your opponent bets 50, what are your pot odds?
exercises.answer: 3 to 1
exercises.explain: Total pot after the bet is 150 (100 + 50). You call 50. So 150 to 50 = 3 to 1.

exercises.question: You have 8 outs on the turn, with one card still to come. What is the chance you hit on the river?
exercises.answer: About 17%
exercises.explain: There are 46 unseen cards (52 minus your 2 and the 4 board cards). 8 outs out of 46 is 17.4%. The 'rule of 4' (outs times 4) is only for two cards to come, such as on the flop. With one card to come, outs times 2 is a rough approximation (16%).

exercises.question: You have 9 outs on the flop, with two cards still to come, and the pot odds are 2 to 1. Is calling profitable by this math alone?
exercises.answer: Yes, about 35% equity beats the 33% needed
exercises.explain: Exactly, the chance of hitting at least one of 9 outs in two cards is 1 minus (38/47 times 37/46), about 35.0%. Pot odds of 2 to 1 mean you must win 1 time in 3 (33.3%) to break even. 35% is slightly above that. The rule of 4 would give 36%, a quick approximation.
choices: Yes, about 35% equity beats the 33% needed
No, you need at least 50% equity
Yes, because 2 to 1 odds always win

exercises.question: You have 6 outs on the flop, with two cards still to come, and the pot odds are 4 to 1. Is calling profitable by this math alone?
exercises.answer: Yes, about 24% equity beats the 20% needed
exercises.explain: Exactly, the chance of hitting at least one of 6 outs in two cards is 1 minus (41/47 times 40/46), about 24.1%. Pot odds of 4 to 1 mean you must win 1 time in 5 (20%) to break even. 24% is above that. The rule of 4 gives 24%, a quick approximation.
choices: Yes, about 24% equity beats the 20% needed
No, you need at least 30% equity
Yes, because 4 to 1 odds always win

units.title: Betting Strategy
units.tip: There are two reasons to bet: to win the pot immediately or to get more money in when you have the best hand. A value bet wins money from worse hands. A bluff wins the pot when you are behind. Position, hand strength, and the board texture determine your strategy.

exercises.question: What is a value bet?
exercises.answer: A bet made when you believe your hand is the strongest
exercises.explain: A value bet aims to get called by weaker hands. If you have a pair and bet, you want your opponent to call with a weaker pair or a draw.
choices: A bet made when you believe your hand is the strongest
A bet equal to the blinds

exercises.question: What is a bluff?
exercises.answer: A bet made when you do not have the best hand, hoping everyone folds
exercises.explain: A bluff tries to win the pot without a showdown. You are betting weak or nothing, but representing strength to convince others to fold.
choices: A bet made when you do not have the best hand, hoping everyone folds
A call instead of a raise
A bet with a strong hand

exercises.question: When is a bluff most likely to work?
exercises.answer: When your opponent has a weak hand and the board looks dangerous
exercises.explain: A bluff works when your opponent is likely to fold. A scary board (lots of cards that could have helped you) makes opponents more likely to fold.
choices: When your opponent has a weak hand and the board looks dangerous

exercises.question: What is a semi-bluff?
exercises.answer: A bet that can win now and has equity if called
exercises.explain: A semi-bluff like a flush draw has a plan: win now, or make a hand later. You are not purely bluffing because your hand can improve.
choices: A bet that can win now and has equity if called
A bet that has no chance of winning
A fold disguised as a bet

exercises.question: Why do strong players mix some bluffs in with their value bets?
exercises.answer: So opponents cannot tell from a bet alone whether the hand is strong
exercises.explain: If a player only bet with the best hand, opponents would simply fold every time. Mixing in some weaker hands makes bets harder to read.
choices: Because strong hands should never bet
So opponents cannot tell from a bet alone whether the hand is strong

exercises.question: What bet size is a common rule of thumb for a value bet?
exercises.answer: About 50% to 100% of the pot
exercises.explain: Many players size value bets at roughly half the pot to the full pot. This is an approximation, not a rule: smaller bets get called more often, larger bets win more when called.
choices: Always the size of the big blind

exercises.question: What does it mean to check?
exercises.answer: Passing your turn to act without betting
exercises.explain: A check is a free action. If everyone checks, the next card is dealt. Checks happen when no one has bet yet in a round.
choices: Passing your turn to act without betting

exercises.question: Which is a common reason to check?
exercises.answer: To see the next card cheaply with a mediocre hand
exercises.explain: A check is only possible when no one has bet yet in that round. Players check with mediocre hands to see the next card without adding chips, or sometimes to hide the strength of a strong hand.
choices: Because checking is required with the best hand
To see the next card cheaply with a mediocre hand

exercises.question: What is a fold?
exercises.answer: Surrendering your hand and losing any money already bet
exercises.explain: When you fold, you leave the hand. You cannot win the pot, but you also lose nothing further.
choices: Surrendering your hand and losing any money already bet

exercises.question: When should you fold?
exercises.answer: When your hand is unlikely to win and your odds do not justify the cost
exercises.explain: Fold when the hand is unlikely to win and the pot odds do not justify the price of a call. Folding means you put no more chips in.
choices: When your hand is unlikely to win and your odds do not justify the cost
Never fold to build your image

units.title: Game Concepts and Discipline
units.tip: Poker is a game of incomplete information. Decisions are made without seeing the opponent's hand. Over a long run, sound decisions tend to do better than bad ones, but short runs are dominated by luck. Treating the game as entertainment, with strict limits, and keeping emotions in check keeps the focus on the math, not the feelings.

exercises.question: What does it mean to read the board?
exercises.answer: Thinking about what hands your opponents might have based on the community cards
exercises.explain: Reading the board means analyzing which hands are possible. A board of 10-10-5 means a player could hold three 10s or a high pocket pair. A dry board such as K-7-2 in mixed suits leaves few strong possibilities.
choices: Thinking about what hands your opponents might have based on the community cards
Counting the cards in the deck

exercises.question: What is a wet board?
exercises.answer: A board with many connected or coordinated cards, creating many possible hands
exercises.explain: A wet board like 9-8-7 creates many straight possibilities, and with two or three of a suit also flush draws. A dry board like K-7-2 in mixed suits has far fewer.
choices: A board with water on it
A board with no face cards
A board where you are losing
A board with many connected or coordinated cards, creating many possible hands

exercises.question: What is a dry board?
exercises.answer: A board with disconnected, uncoordinated cards, few possibilities
exercises.explain: A dry board like K-7-2 in mixed suits has few connections. Straights and flushes are very unlikely, so players usually have high card, a single pair, or a weak draw.
choices: A board with disconnected, uncoordinated cards, few possibilities
A board where you always win
A board of all low cards
A board with three of a kind

exercises.question: If the board is K-Q-J-9, what is a big concern?
exercises.answer: Your opponent might have made a straight with a 10
exercises.explain: A 10 makes a straight (10-J-Q-K-9) on this board. This is a wet, connected board that creates many strong hands.
choices: Your opponent might have made a straight with a 10

exercises.question: On the board A-A-5-2, which two-card hand makes a full house?
exercises.explain: 5-5 plus the board gives 5-5-5-A-A, a full house. K-K makes only two pair, K-Q makes only a pair of Aces, and 7-6 makes a pair of Aces too. (A-K would make three Aces, not a full house.)

exercises.question: What is bankroll management?
exercises.answer: Playing within your means so one downswing does not wipe you out
exercises.explain: A bankroll is a fixed amount set aside for the game. Managing it means keeping stakes small compared with it, so a normal run of bad luck does not end play.
choices: Playing within your means so one downswing does not wipe you out

exercises.question: What is tilt?
exercises.answer: Losing emotional control and making bad decisions due to frustration
exercises.explain: Tilt is when a player acts on emotion instead of math. Bad beats or losses can cause it, and players on tilt tend to make larger bets and worse decisions.
choices: Losing emotional control and making bad decisions due to frustration

exercises.question: How can you avoid tilt?
exercises.answer: Take breaks, stay calm, and focus on making good decisions
exercises.explain: When frustrated, step away from the game. Remind yourself that bad beats happen to everyone. Focus on the math, not the outcome.
choices: Take breaks, stay calm, and focus on making good decisions

exercises.question: What is variance?
exercises.answer: Natural short-term swings in your results due to luck
exercises.explain: Even good players lose streaks because of variance. You can play perfectly and still lose in the short term. Variance averages out over many hands.
choices: Natural short-term swings in your results due to luck

exercises.question: Which mindset do strong players aim for?
exercises.answer: Judging each decision by its quality, not by one result
exercises.explain: A good decision can lose and a bad one can win in the short term. Judging plays by the math rather than the outcome helps keep emotions from driving choices.
choices: Only playing when holding strong cards
Assuming a win means the play was right
Judging each decision by its quality, not by one result
